fields.title: Business model: how a product turns value into revenue
fields.keyTakeaway: A business model is an interconnected web: target audience, value proposition, channels, monetization engine, and cost drivers. It is validated via unit economics — analyzing revenue and cost per customer, not aggregate revenue.
fields.checkQuestion: Revenue is growing, but cash on hand is shrinking. Which two numbers should you check first?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how does the product monetize value?** In section S2, we analyzed markets and customer segments; here, we focus on translating them into a sustainable business model.
fields.blocks/1/text: Running example: Kedr is a fictional cloud warehouse WMS for small distributors, 120 clients, 40 thousand rubles per month subscription fee.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Nine building blocks; focus on interdependencies
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Customer segments** and **Value proposition** — who you serve and what value you deliver.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Channels** and **Customer relationships** — how you reach and retain customers.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Revenue streams** — what clients pay for and what value metric is used: per seat, per location, or per volume.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Key resources, Key activities, and Key partners** — core internal competencies versus external integrations.
fields.blocks/2/items/4: **Cost structure** — fixed vs. variable costs, isolating expenses that scale with customer count.
fields.blocks/2/items/5: **Validation:** shifting one block impacts adjacent ones. Moving to channel partners changes both pricing structure and cost dynamics.
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: Calculated per customer unit, not at company scale
fields.blocks/3/items/0: **LTV per client** — average recurring payment multiplied by average lifetime.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: **Variable costs** — incremental expenses per client: hosting, support, commissions, onboarding.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: **Contribution margin per unit** = LTV minus variable costs. If negative, scaling amplifies cash drain.
fields.blocks/3/items/3: **CAC and Payback Period** — acquisition cost and months to break even on acquisition spend.
fields.blocks/3/items/4: **Fixed overhead** is covered by cumulative contribution margin: dictates unit count needed to reach breakeven.
fields.blocks/4/text:
Average client: 40,000 ₽/month, 26 months tenure → 1,040,000 ₽ LTV.
Variable costs: cloud hosting 3,000 ₽/month, support 4,000 ₽/month, onboarding 60,000 ₽ one-time → 242,000 ₽ over lifespan.
Contribution margin: 798,000 ₽. CAC: 180,000 ₽ (direct sales, two-month cycle). Payback period: ~5.5 months.

However, segmented view paints a different picture: retail chains run 21,000 ₽/month in support plus custom dev, driving contribution margin negative; manufacturers churn at 5 months, failing to pay back CAC.

The blended average looked healthy, masking two money-losing segments.
fields.blocks/5/text: Clients pay monthly while customer acquisition and onboarding are paid upfront. Faster growth widens this working capital gap: this is cash flow crunch, not unprofitability, solved by annual prepayments, onboarding fees, or working capital financing.
fields.blocks/5/title: Revenue grows while cash shrinks — usually a cash flow timing issue
fields.blocks/6/text: Unit economics for early-stage products rely on assumed LTV retention figures that lack historical proof. It is safer to calculate economics based strictly on observed cohorts and recalculate quarterly.
